title: LRU Cache
scopeHtml: Scope: HashMap plus doubly linked list in O(1), sentinels, Decorator for thread safety, LFU in O(1), lock striping, stampede, TTL and aging follow-ups.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a fixed-size cache that throws away the "least recently used" entry when full, with O(1) get and put. Then extend it to LFU (least frequently used).

Ask these before coding: is it generic (any key and value types)? Fixed capacity? What do get of a missing key and put of an existing key do? Does it need to be thread-safe? Is there a TTL? (Here: generic, fixed capacity, get returns null on miss, put on an existing key updates and refreshes it, thread-safety as a follow-up, no TTL.)

Worked example. Capacity 2. put(a), put(b), get(a), put(c). After get(a), a is the freshest and b the stalest, so put(c) evicts b. A naive "scan for the oldest timestamp" costs O(n) per eviction; with a 1M-entry cache and 50k puts/s that is 50 billion steps/s, impossible. We need O(1).

Industry examples. Guava CacheBuilder, Caffeine (uses W-TinyLFU, a smarter LFU/LRU mix), Redis maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru (approximate LRU: samples a few keys, evicts the oldest of the sample, to save memory), Android android.util.LruCache for bitmaps, the Linux page cache.

Everyday analogy. A small desk that fits 5 books. When you need a 6th, you put back the one you have not touched for longest.

Common interview traps.

  • Using only a HashMap plus timestamps (O(n) eviction).
  • Using LinkedHashMap(accessOrder=true) and stopping there. It is a valid shortcut (override removeEldestEntry), mention it, but the interviewer usually wants you to build the list yourself.
  • Forgetting that get changes state (recency), which matters for thread safety later.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
Three pieces only:

  • Cache<K,V> interface: get, put, size. Callers depend on this, so LRU, LFU and a thread-safe wrapper are interchangeable.
  • Node: holds key, value, prev, next. The key is stored in the node so that when we evict the tail we know which map entry to delete.
  • HashMap<K, Node> for O(1) lookup, plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency (head = freshest, tail = stalest).

Why both? A map finds a node in O(1) but has no order. A list keeps order and removes a known node in O(1) (if doubly linked) but cannot find one without scanning. Together: find via map, reorder via list.

Decision gravity. The data-structure choice is internal behind the Cache interface, so it is reversible (a two-way door). The interface itself is the one to get right early because many callers depend on it.

Everyday analogy. A library index (map) tells you which shelf slot a book is in; the shelf itself (list) is where you move the book you just used to the front.

Common interview traps.

  • A singly linked list: removing a node from the middle needs its predecessor, which is O(n).
  • Not storing the key in the node, so eviction cannot remove the map entry.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
<<interface>>
   +--------------------+
   |  Cache<K,V>        |
   |  get(K): V         |
   |  put(K,V)          |
   |  size(): int       |
   +--------------------+
      ^         ^          ^
      |         |          |
+-----------+ +-----------+ +--------------------+
| LRUCache  | | LFUCache  | | SynchronizedCache  |
| map       | | vals      | | inner: Cache  -----+--> wraps any Cache
| head,tail | | freq      | | (Decorator)        |
| capacity  | | buckets   | +--------------------+
+-----------+ | minFreq   |
   | has many +-----------+
   v
+---------------------+
| Node: key,val,prev, |
|       next          |
+---------------------+

List order:  head <-> [freshest] <-> ... <-> [stalest] <-> tail

How to read it. head and tail are dummy sentinel nodes, so inserting and removing never needs null checks. The real LRU victim is always tail.prev.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the sentinels; the code then fills with if (head == null) branches.
  • Making LRUCache itself synchronized. Better to keep it simple and wrap it (Decorator) so single-threaded users pay nothing.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Decorator (SynchronizedCache): adds locking around any Cache without changing it. Why: thread safety is a separate concern; single-threaded callers should not pay. Alternative: put synchronized inside LRUCache (simpler, cannot be turned off). Breaks when one global lock becomes the bottleneck (see Concurrency). Reversible.
  • Strategy (eviction policy): LRU and LFU are two policies behind one interface. In a bigger design you would split EvictionPolicy (onAccess, evict) from storage so a Guava-style cache can swap policy by config. Not done here: for one interview, two classes are clearer than three abstractions.
  • Sentinel nodes: removes edge cases; a coding technique, not a GoF pattern.

Industry examples. Caffeine and Guava build an eviction policy + storage + stats + loader pipeline; Redis picks a policy via config; the JDK's own LinkedHashMap is the built-in LRU.

Everyday analogy. A bouncer (decorator) in front of a club: the club (cache) works the same; the bouncer only lets one person through the door at a time.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming patterns without saying what problem each solves.
  • Adding an EvictionPolicy hierarchy, a CacheBuilder and a StatsCounter in a 45-minute round. Offer them as extensions instead.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Full runnable file Main.java (LRU, synchronized wrapper, LFU and a test in main):

import java.util.*;

interface Cache<K, V> {
    V get(K key);
    void put(K key, V value);
    int size();
}

/** O(1) get/put: HashMap for lookup + doubly linked list for recency order. NOT thread-safe. */
class LRUCache<K, V> implements Cache<K, V> {
    private class Node {
        K key; V val; Node prev, next;
        Node(K k, V v) { key = k; val = v; }
    }
    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<K, Node> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final Node head = new Node(null, null), tail = new Node(null, null); // sentinels

    LRUCache(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be > 0");
        this.capacity = capacity;
        head.next = tail; tail.prev = head;
    }
    public V get(K key) {
        Node n = map.get(key);
        if (n == null) return null;
        unlink(n); addFront(n);              // a read makes it most recent
        return n.val;
    }
    public void put(K key, V value) {
        Node n = map.get(key);
        if (n != null) { n.val = value; unlink(n); addFront(n); return; }
        if (map.size() == capacity) {        // evict least recently used = node before tail
            Node lru = tail.prev;
            unlink(lru); map.remove(lru.key);
        }
        n = new Node(key, value);
        map.put(key, n); addFront(n);
    }
    public int size() { return map.size(); }
    private void unlink(Node n) { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; }
    private void addFront(Node n) {
        n.next = head.next; n.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = n; head.next = n;
    }
}

/** Thread-safe decorator: get() mutates order, so even reads need the lock. */
class SynchronizedCache<K, V> implements Cache<K, V> {
    private final Cache<K, V> inner;
    SynchronizedCache(Cache<K, V> inner) { this.inner = inner; }
    public synchronized V get(K key) { return inner.get(key); }
    public synchronized void put(K key, V value) { inner.put(key, value); }
    public synchronized int size() { return inner.size(); }
}

/** LFU follow-up, O(1): key->value, key->freq, freq->keys in insertion order, plus minFreq. */
class LFUCache<K, V> implements Cache<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<K, V> vals = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<K, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<Integer, LinkedHashSet<K>> buckets = new HashMap<>();
    private int minFreq = 0;

    LFUCache(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be > 0");
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }
    public V get(K key) {
        if (!vals.containsKey(key)) return null;
        touch(key);
        return vals.get(key);
    }
    public void put(K key, V value) {
        if (vals.containsKey(key)) { vals.put(key, value); touch(key); return; }
        if (vals.size() == capacity) {       // evict lowest freq; ties -> oldest (LRU) in that bucket
            LinkedHashSet<K> set = buckets.get(minFreq);
            K victim = set.iterator().next();
            set.remove(victim);
            vals.remove(victim); freq.remove(victim);
        }
        vals.put(key, value); freq.put(key, 1);
        buckets.computeIfAbsent(1, f -> new LinkedHashSet<>()).add(key);
        minFreq = 1;
    }
    public int size() { return vals.size(); }
    private void touch(K key) {
        int f = freq.get(key);
        LinkedHashSet<K> set = buckets.get(f);
        set.remove(key);
        if (set.isEmpty() && minFreq == f) minFreq = f + 1;
        freq.put(key, f + 1);
        buckets.computeIfAbsent(f + 1, x -> new LinkedHashSet<>()).add(key);
    }
}

public class Main {
    static void check(boolean c, String msg) { if (!c) throw new AssertionError(msg); }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Cache<String, Integer> lru = new LRUCache<>(2);
        lru.put("a", 1); lru.put("b", 2);
        lru.get("a");                 // a is now most recent
        lru.put("c", 3);              // evicts b
        check(lru.get("b") == null && lru.get("a") == 1 && lru.get("c") == 3, "LRU eviction");

        Cache<String, Integer> lfu = new LFUCache<>(2);
        lfu.put("a", 1); lfu.put("b", 2);
        lfu.get("a"); lfu.get("a");   // a freq 3, b freq 1
        lfu.put("c", 3);              // evicts b (lowest freq)
        check(lfu.get("b") == null && lfu.get("a") == 1, "LFU eviction");

        // concurrency: 8 threads hammer a synchronized cache; size must never exceed capacity
        Cache<Integer, Integer> safe = new SynchronizedCache<>(new LRUCache<>(100));
        Thread[] ts = new Thread[8];
        for (int t = 0; t < ts.length; t++) {
            final int id = t;
            ts[t] = new Thread(() -> {
                Random r = new Random(id);
                for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                    int k = r.nextInt(500);
                    if (r.nextBoolean()) safe.put(k, k); else safe.get(k);
                }
            });
            ts[t].start();
        }
        for (Thread t : ts) t.join();
        check(safe.size() <= 100, "capacity respected under contention");
        System.out.println("P7 OK, size=" + safe.size());
    }
}

The same core in Kotlin (LRU; the rest follows identically):

class LRUCache<K : Any, V>(private val capacity: Int) {
    private class Node<K, V>(val key: K?, var value: V?) {
        var prev: Node<K, V>? = null
        var next: Node<K, V>? = null
    }
    private val map = HashMap<K, Node<K, V>>()
    private val head = Node<K, V>(null, null)
    private val tail = Node<K, V>(null, null)

    init {
        require(capacity > 0)
        head.next = tail; tail.prev = head
    }

    @Synchronized fun get(key: K): V? {
        val n = map[key] ?: return null
        unlink(n); addFront(n)
        return n.value
    }

    @Synchronized fun put(key: K, value: V) {
        map[key]?.let { it.value = value; unlink(it); addFront(it); return }
        if (map.size == capacity) {
            val lru = tail.prev!!
            unlink(lru); map.remove(lru.key)
        }
        val n = Node(key, value)
        map[key] = n; addFront(n)
    }

    private fun unlink(n: Node<K, V>) { n.prev!!.next = n.next; n.next!!.prev = n.prev }
    private fun addFront(n: Node<K, V>) {
        n.next = head.next; n.prev = head
        head.next!!.prev = n; head.next = n
    }
}

// Shortcut worth knowing (JVM): LinkedHashMap does exactly this
fun <K, V> lru(cap: Int) = object : LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) {
    override fun removeEldestEntry(e: MutableMap.MutableEntry<K, V>) = size > cap
}

How get and put work. get: map lookup, unlink the node, add it at the front. put of a new key when full: remove tail.prev, delete its map entry, then insert the new node at the front. Each step is a handful of pointer writes, so O(1).

LFU idea. Keep a frequency per key, and for each frequency a LinkedHashSet of keys (insertion order = recency among ties). Track minFreq. Evict the oldest key of the minFreq bucket; touching a key moves it from bucket f to f+1, and if bucket minFreq became empty, minFreq++. A new key always has frequency 1, so minFreq resets to 1.

LFU state after: put a, put b, get a, get a
vals     : a=1, b=2
freq     : a=3, b=1
buckets  : 1 -> [b]     3 -> [a]
minFreq  : 1     -> put c evicts b

Common interview traps.

  • Updating an existing key without moving it to the front.
  • LFU tie-breaking left undefined; say "among equal frequency, evict the least recently used".
  • LFU with a PriorityQueue: O(log n) and stale entries; the bucket design is O(1).

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac Main.java && java -ea Main
# prints: P7 OK, size=100

-ea enables the check assertions. The test covers: LRU evicts the right key after a get refresh; LFU evicts the lowest-frequency key; 8 threads doing 800,000 random operations never push a synchronized cache above capacity 100.

In a real project (JUnit) you would add: put on an existing key refreshes order; capacity 1; a null-value policy; an eviction callback; repeated stress runs.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "I tested it" without a walk-through. Do a dry run on the board with capacity 2 and 4 operations.
  • Not testing capacity 1 (sentinel edge case).

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
The trap: get is a write. It reorders the list, so even read-only callers mutate shared state. A ReadWriteLock does not help (reads need the write lock), and a plain HashMap read concurrent with a write can corrupt it (the classic pre-Java-8 symptom: 100% CPU stuck in HashMap.get).

Three levels, simplest to best:

  1. One lock (the synchronized wrapper above). Correct and simple. Under heavy multi-thread load all callers queue on one lock, so throughput flattens at a few million ops/s.
  2. Lock striping. Hash the key to one of 16 or 64 segments, each its own small LRU with its own lock. Contention drops roughly by the segment count; the price is that LRU becomes approximate (per segment, not global). Older Guava (concurrencyLevel, default 4) worked this way.
  3. Buffered recency (Caffeine). Reads hit a ConcurrentHashMap without locking and just record the access in a lock-free buffer; a maintenance task replays those records to reorder the list. Reads become nearly lock-free. Cost: eviction order lags slightly.
// Level 2 sketch: independent shards
class ShardedCache<K, V> {
    private final Cache<K, V>[] shards;
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    ShardedCache(int n, int capPerShard) {
        shards = new Cache[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) shards[i] = new SynchronizedCache<>(new LRUCache<>(capPerShard));
    }
    private Cache<K, V> shard(K k) { return shards[(k.hashCode() & 0x7fffffff) % shards.length]; }
    V get(K k) { return shard(k).get(k); }
    void put(K k, V v) { shard(k).put(k, v); }
}

Cache stampede (a production incident). When a hot key expires, 1,000 requests miss at once and all hit the database. Symptom: DB CPU spikes right after a deploy that cleared the cache; the metric that shows it is the cache hit ratio dropping from about 98% to near 0%. Fixes: per-key single flight (first caller loads, others wait), jittered TTLs, or serve stale while refreshing (Caffeine refreshAfterWrite).

Decision gravity. Starting with one lock is correct and reversible. Moving to striping changes eviction semantics (approximate global LRU), so tell callers; treat it as a one-way-ish door if anything depends on exact order.

Everyday analogy. One cashier (single lock) versus several checkout lanes (striping). Lanes are faster, but "the single longest-waiting customer goes first" is no longer guaranteed.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "use ConcurrentHashMap" and forgetting the list must be updated atomically with the map.
  • Synchronizing only put. Both get and put mutate.
  • Holding the lock while loading from the database on a miss; loads must happen outside the lock.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• TTL expiry: store expiresAt in the Node; check lazily on get, and sweep with a scheduled task.
  • LFU frequency aging: classic LFU never forgets old popularity. TinyLFU/Caffeine halve counters periodically; Redis LFU uses a logarithmic counter that decays (lfu-decay-time).
  • Cache-aside vs read-through: a loader function (computeIfAbsent style) lets the cache fetch misses itself.
  • Write policies: write-through, write-back (risk of loss), write-around.
  • Distributed: consistent hashing across cache nodes (Memcached clients, Redis Cluster slots); see the HLD caching topics.
  • Memory limit instead of count: weigh entries by byte size (Caffeine maximumWeight).

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to distributed caches before finishing the single-node version.
  • Forgetting an eviction listener when entries hold resources (file handles, bitmaps).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• LRU = HashMap for lookup + doubly linked list for order, with sentinel head/tail. All operations O(1).
  • get mutates recency, so thread safety needs the write lock even for reads; wrap with a Decorator.
  • LFU in O(1): key to freq, freq to ordered key set, plus minFreq; ties broken by recency.
  • Scale locking in steps: one lock, then striping, then buffered recency (Caffeine).
  • Mention the stampede problem and TTL jitter; they show production experience.

questions.promptHtml: Why does an O(1) LRU cache need both a HashMap and a doubly linked list? Why not just one of them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the core insight of the problem; candidates who only memorise code cannot defend the structure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The map finds a node in O(1) but has no order. The list keeps recency order and can unlink a known node in O(1) because it is doubly linked, but it cannot find a node without scanning. Together: map to find, list to reorder and to find the victim at the tail. The node stores its key so that evicting the tail can also delete the map entry.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
map:  key -> Node
list: head <-> [freshest] <-> ... <-> [stalest] <-> tail     (head, tail are sentinels)
get(k):  node = map[k]; unlink(node); addFront(node)
put(k):  full? victim = tail.prev; unlink(victim); map.remove(victim.key)

A singly linked list makes unlink O(n) because you need the predecessor. A plain map with timestamps makes eviction O(n) (scan for the oldest). Sentinels remove every null check for first and last element, so unlink and addFront are four pointer writes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
private void unlink(Node n) { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; }
private void addFront(Node n) {
    n.next = head.next; n.prev = head;
    head.next.prev = n; head.next = n;
}
private fun unlink(n: Node<K, V>) { n.prev!!.next = n.next; n.next!!.prev = n.prev }
private fun addFront(n: Node<K, V>) {
    n.next = head.next; n.prev = head
    head.next!!.prev = n; head.next = n
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Singly linked list (O(n) removal).
  • Node without the key, so the map entry cannot be removed on eviction.
  • No sentinels; the code fills with head == null branches.
  • Forgetting that put of an existing key must also refresh recency.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you do it with LinkedHashMap? -> Yes: accessOrder=true and override removeEldestEntry; mention it, then build it by hand if asked.
  2. What is the space overhead? -> Per entry: one map entry plus one node with two pointers.
  3. How would you make it generic and null-safe? -> Generics <K,V>, get returns null on miss (or Optional); reject null keys.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer recites "hashmap and linked list". The senior explains what each structure cannot do, why doubly, why the key lives in the node, and offers LinkedHashMap as the production shortcut.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Android LruCache and Guava/Caffeine caches use the same idea, with extra layers for concurrency.

questions.promptHtml: How do you build an LFU cache with O(1) get and put? How do you break ties, and why is a PriorityQueue the wrong tool?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you can extend a design: three maps and one integer, and the subtle minFreq rule.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep vals (key to value), freq (key to count) and buckets (count to an insertion-ordered set of keys), plus minFreq. Get or put bumps a key from bucket f to f+1; if bucket minFreq became empty, minFreq increases. A new key is always frequency 1, so minFreq resets to 1. Evict the oldest key in bucket minFreq, which makes ties break by least recently used.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
after: put a, put b, get a, get a
vals    : a=1, b=2
freq    : a=3, b=1
buckets : 1 -> [b]    3 -> [a]
minFreq : 1           -> put c evicts b

A PriorityQueue keyed by frequency has O(log n) updates and stale entries when frequency changes (you would have to remove and re-add), so it fails the O(1) requirement. LinkedHashSet gives O(1) remove and oldest-first iteration.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
private void touch(K key) {
    int f = freq.get(key);
    LinkedHashSet<K> set = buckets.get(f);
    set.remove(key);
    if (set.isEmpty() && minFreq == f) minFreq = f + 1;
    freq.put(key, f + 1);
    buckets.computeIfAbsent(f + 1, x -> new LinkedHashSet<>()).add(key);
}
private fun touch(key: K) {
    val f = freq.getValue(key)
    val set = buckets.getValue(f)
    set.remove(key)
    if (set.isEmpty() && minFreq == f) minFreq = f + 1
    freq[key] = f + 1
    buckets.getOrPut(f + 1) { LinkedHashSet() }.add(key)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving ties undefined; say "among equal frequency, evict the least recently used".
  • Forgetting minFreq = 1 on insert, or not advancing it when the bucket empties.
  • Updating an existing key's value without touching its frequency.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does classic LFU suffer? -> Old popularity never decays; a once-hot key sticks forever.
  2. What do real caches do? -> TinyLFU/Caffeine halve counters periodically; Redis uses a decaying logarithmic counter (lfu-decay-time).
  3. Capacity 0 or 1? -> Reject 0; with 1 every put of a new key evicts the only entry.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer proposes a heap. The senior shows the bucket structure, the minFreq invariant, the tie-break, and names the aging problem.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An LFU-only cache kept yesterday's viral items and starved today's; adding decay fixed the hit ratio.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate's LRU passes the basic test but production shows the wrong items evicted. Capacity 2. Sequence: put(a,1), put(b,2), put(a,10), put(c,3), then get(a) returns null, although a was just updated.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public void put(K key, V value) {
    Node n = map.get(key);
    if (n != null) { n.val = value; return; }          // existing key
    if (map.size() == capacity) {
        Node lru = tail.prev;
        map.remove(lru.key);                            // unlink missing
    }
    n = new Node(key, value);
    map.put(key, n); addFront(n);
}
fun put(key: K, value: V) {
    map[key]?.let { it.value = value; return }          // existing key
    if (map.size == capacity) {
        val lru = tail.prev!!
        map.remove(lru.key)                              // unlink missing
    }
    val n = Node(key, value)
    map[key] = n; addFront(n)
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every bug and say how you would test for each.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Finds only the missing refresh, not the unlink omission that leaves a ghost node in the list.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What should put on an existing key do (update and make freshest)? Is capacity validated?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; block the merge and add the failing tests.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) updating an existing key does not move it to the front, so a stays stale and is evicted; (b) on eviction the node is removed from the map but not unlinked from the list, so tail.prev still points at the dead node and later evictions pick the same victim, the map and list diverge, and size stops matching; (c) no capacity validation.
  4. How I'd verify: Walk the sequence: after put(a,10) the list is still b (freshest) then a (stalest)? put(c) evicts a. A second eviction removes the same ghost node. Tests: update-refreshes, eviction removes exactly one node and the list length equals the map size, capacity 1.
  5. Root cause: Two structures must change together; each operation updated only one.
  6. Fix: Update path: n.val = value; unlink(n); addFront(n);. Eviction path: unlink(lru); map.remove(lru.key);.
  7. Prevention: An invariant check in tests (walk the list, count equals map.size()), and property tests with random operations compared against LinkedHashMap.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not patch by scanning the list; it must stay O(1).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• get on a miss, should it create an entry? -> No, return null; loaders belong to read-through variants.
  • Null values? -> Decide and document, or reject with an exception.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cache shrank to half its capacity over days because ghost nodes kept being chosen as victims; a model-based test against LinkedHashMap found it in a minute.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves or finds no bug.
  • Hire: finds both missing-refresh and missing-unlink.
  • Strong hire: adds invariant and model-based tests.

questions.contextHtml:
After a deploy that restarted all 12 app servers, the product-page API p99 went from 40 ms to 9 s for four minutes. Metrics: cache hit ratio 98% to 3%, DB CPU 100%, DB connections at max 200, normal peak 4,000 req/s to the app with 1,000 of them for 20 hot products.

12:00:00 deploy complete, cache empty
12:00:01 hit_ratio=0.03 db_active=198 qps_db=3,900
12:00:20 db_cpu=100% p99=9.1s
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure, how you stop it now, and how you prevent a repeat.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the DB size." Treats the symptom; and without single flight the same hot keys are still loaded thousands of times at once.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the cache in-process or shared (Redis)? Do TTLs expire together? Is there a loader with a lock? Can we warm it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed or rate-limit traffic, serve stale pages where possible, roll traffic in gradually (a few servers at a time).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) cold cache stampede on hot keys: 1,000 requests miss the same 20 keys and each hits the DB; (b) in-process cache per server multiplies misses by 12; (c) a slow query. Red herring: GC pauses; DB CPU says otherwise.
  4. How I'd verify: Count DB queries per product id in the slow log; many identical queries at the same millisecond confirm a stampede. Compare hit ratio per key.
  5. Root cause: On a miss every caller loads independently; nothing coalesces them.
  6. Fix: Single flight per key: the first caller loads, others wait on the same future. Jitter TTLs. Pre-warm hot keys before taking traffic. Stale-while-revalidate (Caffeine refreshAfterWrite). Load outside the cache lock.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
V get(K key) {
    return inflight.computeIfAbsent(key, k ->
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> loader.load(k))
            .whenComplete((v, e) -> inflight.remove(k))).join();
}
fun get(key: K): V =
    inflight.computeIfAbsent(key) { k ->
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { loader.load(k) }
            .whenComplete { _, _ -> inflight.remove(k) }
    }.join()
  1. Prevention: Canary deploys with warm-up, alert on hit ratio drop, load test with a cold start.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not hold the cache lock while loading; one slow load would block all keys. Stale serving trades freshness for stability.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The loader fails? -> Do not cache the failure for long; short negative cache plus backoff.
  • Across 12 servers? -> Add a shared cache layer or a per-key distributed lock; local single flight only collapses within a process.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A routine restart took the database down because 20 homepage keys were each loaded 600 times; single flight reduced DB load by two orders of magnitude.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale the database.
  • Hire: single flight, jitter, warm-up.
  • Strong hire: ties it to the deploy, per-process multiplication, stale-while-revalidate, and reasons about the loader outside the lock.

questions.contextHtml: Your LRU cache is used for user sessions (1M entries, count-bounded). Two requests arrive: (1) entries must expire 30 minutes after write, even if hot; (2) when an entry is evicted or expires, a session holding an open file handle must be closed. Today LRUCache has no hooks, and Node holds only key, value, prev, next.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes and fields change, and how do you keep O(1) operations and thread safety?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds a timer thread per entry, or scans all entries every minute under the lock.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is expiry strict or best effort? Is TTL per cache or per entry? Must the close run synchronously? What if close is slow or throws?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; ship the listener first, since leaked handles are the live risk.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (designs): (a) expiresAt in Node, checked lazily on get, plus a scheduled sweeper; (b) per-entry timers (too heavy); (c) a time-ordered queue or timer wheel for the sweeper.
  4. How I'd verify: Fake clock tests: entry expires at exactly 30 min, get after expiry returns null and fires the listener once; eviction fires the listener; an exception in the listener does not corrupt the list.
  5. Root cause of the gap: The cache owns lifetime now, so it must own cleanup.
  6. Fix: Add expiresAt to Node, a LongSupplier clock, and an EvictionListener<K,V> interface called on eviction, expiry and explicit removal, after unlinking. get checks clock >= expiresAt, removes and notifies. A sweeper takes a batch from a time-ordered structure (or scans a bounded slice each tick) so the lock is held briefly. Run listeners outside the lock (collect victims, release the lock, then notify).
  7. Prevention: Test that the sweeper never holds the lock longer than X ms; metrics: evictions by reason (size, expiry, explicit).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not calling slow close code inside the synchronized block. Lazy expiry is correct on its own; the sweeper only reclaims memory.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Different TTL per entry? -> Store expiresAt per node; ordering by expiry needs a second structure (heap or timer wheel).
  • Listener throws? -> Catch and log; never let it break the cache.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: File descriptors ran out on a session service because evicted entries were never closed; an eviction listener plus an fd gauge solved it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: timer per entry or full scans under lock.
  • Hire: lazy expiry plus listener.
  • Strong hire: listener outside the lock, sweeper design, fake-clock tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate makes the LRU thread-safe like this, to let "readers run in parallel":

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class RWCache<K, V> implements Cache<K, V> {
    private final LRUCache<K, V> inner;
    private final ReadWriteLock lock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
    public V get(K key) {
        lock.readLock().lock();
        try { return inner.get(key); } finally { lock.readLock().unlock(); }
    }
    public void put(K key, V value) {
        lock.writeLock().lock();
        try { inner.put(key, value); } finally { lock.writeLock().unlock(); }
    }
}
class RWCache<K : Any, V>(private val inner: LRUCache<K, V>) {
    private val lock = ReentrantReadWriteLock()
    fun get(key: K): V? = lock.read { inner.get(key) }
    fun put(key: K, value: V) = lock.write { inner.put(key, value) }
}

Under load: occasional NullPointerException in unlink, size() > capacity assertions fail, and sometimes a thread spins at 100% CPU.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and what would you do instead?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ReadWriteLock is fine; add volatile fields." Misses that get mutates the list.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What throughput is needed (ops/s)? Read/write ratio? Is exact LRU order required?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Swap in the synchronized Decorator, which is correct, and redeploy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) get reorders the list, so multiple readers hold the read lock and mutate prev/next concurrently: corrupt list (the NPE); (b) HashMap plus a concurrent write corrupting links causes the spin; (c) size() counts stale state. Red herring: volatile, which does not make a multi-field update atomic.
  4. How I'd verify: Stress test with 8 threads and random get/put, asserting invariants (list length equals map size, size <= capacity) and jstack for the spinning thread.
  5. Root cause: A read in an LRU is a write; a read lock allows many of them at once.
  6. Fix: One lock for both get and put (Decorator SynchronizedCache). For throughput, stripe into N independent shards (approximate LRU), or use buffered recency (Caffeine style): reads hit a ConcurrentHashMap and enqueue an access record; a maintenance task replays them.
  7. Prevention: A concurrency test in CI with a latch and invariant checks; review rule: any method that reorders state needs the write lock.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not ConcurrentHashMap alone: the list and the map must change atomically. Striping loses exact global LRU; say it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Who holds the lock while loading on a miss? -> Nobody; load outside, then put.
  • Can I use Collections.synchronizedMap(new LinkedHashMap(...))? -> Yes, it works with a single lock, with the same contention limits.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "read-optimised" cache looked fine in tests but corrupted under production concurrency; a pre-Java-8 HashMap infinite loop is the older cousin of the same bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes reads are safe in parallel.
  • Hire: notes get mutates, uses one lock.
  • Strong hire: also proposes sharding/buffering with the exact-order trade-off and an invariant stress test.

questions.contextHtml:
An in-process LRU wrapped in one synchronized lock serves an API on a 16-core box. At 300k lookups/s the lock is fine. A traffic launch will take it to 3M lookups/s (10x), 90% reads. Profiling at 1.5M/s:

cpu: 38% total (16 cores)    context switches: 410k/s
top monitor: SynchronizedCache.get   threads blocked: 41 of 64
p99 get(): 0.3 ms  ->  14 ms
hit ratio 92%, capacity 2M entries
questions.promptHtml: How do you get to 3M ops/s, and what do you give up?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use ConcurrentHashMap." Or "add more servers" without removing the single-lock ceiling per box.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is exact LRU a hard requirement? Is the key distribution skewed (hot keys)? Can memory grow? Can I use a library (Caffeine)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add servers or shed non-critical traffic to buy time; the lock contention is the bottleneck, not CPU.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) one global lock serialising a 90%-read workload; (b) hot keys concentrate traffic on a few lines; (c) the lock holder is descheduled. Red herring: GC, since CPU is only 38%.
  4. How I'd verify: jstack / async-profiler lock profile showing time blocked on the monitor; JFR contended-monitor events; hit ratio as a function of shard count in a replay.
  5. Root cause: get mutates recency so every read takes the write lock; throughput is bounded by one critical section.
  6. Fix: Step 1, lock striping: 64 shards each with its own small LRU (eviction approximate per shard). Step 2, if still hot, buffered recency: lock-free reads from a ConcurrentHashMap, access records replayed by a maintenance thread (Caffeine). In practice I would adopt Caffeine rather than hand-roll.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
private Cache<K, V> shard(K k) { return shards[(k.hashCode() & 0x7fffffff) % shards.length]; }
private fun shard(k: K): Cache<K, V> = shards[(k.hashCode() and 0x7fffffff) % shards.size]
  1. Prevention: Benchmark (JMH) at 2x target load; alert on lock wait and p99; capacity per shard sized with headroom.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Striping makes eviction approximate per shard, and a hot shard evicts earlier; buffered recency delays order updates. I would not use a global read-write lock; it does not help.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One key gets 30% of traffic? -> Shards do not help; add a tiny per-thread/near cache or replicate the hot key.
  • How do you size shards? -> Roughly 4x cores to start, then measure; too many shards waste memory and hurt hit ratio.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving from one lock to 64 shards raised throughput 9x and cost 1.5 points of hit ratio; the team accepted it, then swapped to Caffeine and got both.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "ConcurrentHashMap" or only horizontal scale.
  • Hire: striping with the approximate-LRU trade-off.
  • Strong hire: buffered recency, measurement plan, hot-key curveball answer.

questions.contextHtml:
A catalogue cache (200k entries) uses LFU. After a big sale event ended, the hit ratio fell from 94% to 61% and stays low for days. Items from the sale still occupy the cache; new trending items are evicted immediately after insertion.

eviction_age_p50 of new keys: 9 s     of old sale keys: never
freq histogram: sale keys 5,000-40,000 hits; new keys 1-3 hits

The manager asks: switch to LRU, tune something, or keep LFU?
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and choose, naming whether the decision is reversible.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "LFU is better than LRU because it tracks popularity", ignoring that frequencies never decay.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the access pattern shifting over time? What is the miss cost? Is the cache sized to hold the hot set? Do we have a loader?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Flush or halve the counters (or restart the cache) so sale keys lose their lead; hit ratio recovers immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) LFU frequency pollution: old counts never age; (b) new keys always start at frequency 1 and sit in the lowest bucket, evicted next (the cold-start problem); (c) cache too small. Red herring: a bad TTL.
  4. How I'd verify: Dump frequency histogram and eviction age of new keys (above); replay the access log against LRU, LFU and LFU with decay offline and compare hit ratios.
  5. Root cause: Classic LFU measures all-time popularity, not current popularity.
  6. Fix: Aging: periodically halve all counters, or use a windowed counter; TinyLFU admission with a small LRU window (Caffeine W-TinyLFU) so new keys get a chance. Short term, LRU is the safe choice when the pattern shifts.
  7. Prevention: Track hit ratio per policy in shadow mode; alert on drops after events; capacity tests with shifting workloads.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "just LRU forever": it is scan-vulnerable (one big scan flushes the hot set). The policy is behind the Cache interface, so switching is a two-way door; sizing and TTL are the one-way commitments for downstream services.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A one-time scan of 1M keys? -> LRU is flushed, LFU/TinyLFU resists it.
  • Counter memory per entry? -> A small saturating counter (a few bits) or a sketch (count-min) in TinyLFU.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promo left its items sticky in an LFU cache; a periodic halving of counters restored the hit ratio without changing the capacity.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips policy without diagnosis.
  • Hire: identifies frequency pollution and proposes aging or LRU.
  • Strong hire: replays traffic offline, names TinyLFU/admission, covers scan resistance and reversibility.
